title: Week 1 Results And How Traditional Devs Are Missing The Point
author: bingewavecinema
selftext:
I posted [this prompt sequence](https://github.com/Glitch-Gaming-Platform/AI-Prompts-For-Game-Development) I came up with that allows me to create full games (15 hours of gameplay) from scratch in 2 days, and traditional developers had everything negative to say about it. I get it, but I also think they're missing the point and the power of it and topics like we'll be covering at the [AI Gaming Festival.](https://www.glitch.fun/gameshows/9eadde86-a1b2-4882-86e4-a3e9e2e08814/view/standalone)

* Your core loop sucks!
*  We shouldn't encourage this behavior.
* There is no soul in this.
* Your package manager has too many unused packages.
* You call those AAA graphics?!?!

So, it's now Friday. Here are the gameplay results after about 50 to 100 players:

https://preview.redd.it/gjwye6enhcjh1.png?width=2136&format=png&auto=webp&s=35bd0fa265666e04f23649e4f35db41946c9ebe4

https://preview.redd.it/06056p6shcjh1.jpg?width=2310&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=a65de3681273b1105175c4b636f8c47a8b171946

I'm beginning to understand my players' experience in the game. Not completely awful, but not great either.

And here's the big takeaway they're missing:

* **Monday:** I had an idea for a game.
* **Tuesday:** The idea was completed and implemented with some testing.
* **Friday:** I'm beginning to understand whether my game's core loop is working or not.

Outside of gaming, we call this: *"Fail fast and fail forward"*

Instead of spending years and lots of time and money, in a single week a solo developer can understand whether their core loop is working and whether they should continue pursuing the idea, what they need to iterate on, or scape it. **That's POWERFUL.**

As a developer myself, I empathize and get it. You've spent the past 2–3 years working tirelessly to hone your craft of making games, and it is a craft; make no mistake.

Then suddenly Joe Schmo has surpassed what took you 2 years in just 2 days, and you have every right to be upset.

But here's the truth: the world is changing, and you either catch up or get left behind.

As a developer, you should have the deeper knowledge to surpass whatever Joe Schmo has created by being more precise and more creative.

And here's the silver lining: AI makes prototyping dramatically faster. You should be taking full advantage of it by building, failing fast, and iterating every week.

>**Codex + Design Round 1:** Next, switch over to Codex. Find a game with artwork, design, and colors that you like. Upload those images and use the prompt for generating the rubric. A style guide and quality rubric will be created for your game. This is important if you want your game to maintain consistency in design and have clear direction for improving it. "Make AAA design" is not a direction.  
  
**Claude + Media + Asset Management:** You should not just throw animations, GLB files, sound files, and other assets into your game. There should be structure and a way to optimize how those assets are served, which is critical for a performant game (compression, LODs, etc.). Copy and paste the "Build Optimized Pipeline, Analyze Media" and "Implement Media Pipeline" prompts into Claude. **Codex + Initial Asset Creation:** Now switch back to Codex. If you have an ElevenLabs API key, this is the perfect time to enter it into Codex. Tell it to read the docs and create sound effects and appropriate music loops for your game. Then copy the "Refine Artwork in Blender" prompt and create your first artwork. It will be rough, but you can improve it later  
  
**Claude + First Game Build:** Now switch back to Claude and use both prompts for implementing your game and building out an onboarding process. Onboarding the player is a critical step.  
  
**Codex + Live Testing + Graphics:** Once your game is built by Claude, switch back to Codex and tell it to do live testing. Because Codex has access to your command line, it can directly control your mobile phone or engine, such as Unity, for testing. For browser games, it will use a built-in browser. replies.author: Recoil42

What a bizarre fucking reply, honestly. 

First you keep oscillating between the context of this post and the context of other posts. If it happened here, it happened here, if it happened elsewhere, it happened elsewhere — but right now you're running headlong into a conversation specifically about what OP has said **here**, and it's just fucking bizarre to interject with a damnation of what OP said elsewhere pretending it applies here in a conversation *specifically about what's being said here.* 

Moreover though, you also keep claiming OP elsewhere presented their work literally as "fully finished and ready to ship game with all core features fully implemented" — but now the material pasted repeatedly says things like "initial asset creation", "first game build", and "rough, improvable" artwork. It describes live testing, audits, and further graphical improvements. 

That's not only the opposite of describing a "ready to ship" process, it's as straightforward a description of first-iteration as one can get. 

The only conclusion here is that "AI makes prototyping dramatically faster," (direct quote!) and OP describes using a week to determine whether the core loop works, whether to iterate, or whether to scrap the idea. 

If your argument was "OP sometimes overstates the maturity of these games" it would be defensible, but that's not what you're doing here. 

The current tangent you're on — *"when OP explicitly discusses prototyping, failing fast, testing a core loop and deciding whether to scrap it, we should pretend they're talking about shipping a finished commercial product"* doesn't even make a lick of fucking sense.

comments.author: -svde-
comments.body:
you completely ignored my comment on your last post but i went through a large portion of your code base, and given this one is in a pro-AI community i think it’s even more relevant and important to point out the innumerable issues with you game. so here’s a copy and paste. this is legitimate criticism from a genuine place, you cannot call it blind hate. 

also i did actually play the game. two 15 min sessions since that’s apparently what your platform allowed lol. i have a powerful machine and your game ran absolutely terribly. i can say with even more confidence that there is zero optimization to  
be had here. 

—

look, code however you wanna code but if you don't actually understand how your codebase (or the practice in general) works, then you are gonna come up short on a lot of stuff.  to address your points:

1.	⁠i know this is mostly semantics, but this is absolutely not a full game, even with your definition. it's a bare-minimum feature checklist for the most part. as you said, it's a playable demo.  
2.	⁠you do not by any stretch of the imagination need a backend for a web game...SO many web games, including those with complex architecture utilizing 3js/webgl/even heavier frameworks, are run 100% client-side. there are a number of ways to do this without ever touching a backend, databasing, API, etc. 3js is just a client-side rendering system. games DO need backends mostly when you get into usr auth, cloud based saving/leadboards/community interactivity elements etc. but that is a specific type of game. a list of technical setup does not translate to a playable game, and certainly not to fun.  
3.	⁠cli =/= native capability for an LLM to boot native mobile instrumentaion or perform headless or full access control over a game engine. cli is a transport and control layer.  
4.	⁠i mean this is more just personal outlook but games cannot or should not be run like startups. b2b/b2c may be able to run on utility but games need to be fun and playable.

some other random things

a lot of your code is the pure opposite of optimized. just glancing over it, i founded multiple places where you hardcoded static increment growths for various non-static mechanics, like crop growth. this should be using delta time.

the majority of the UI uses hardcoded raw english string literals in the html/dom elements. meaning you have a ton of random empty key lookups instead of translation func routings. this makes your localization fake.

likewise, the telemetry referenced in analytics.ts manually logs msgs to console.log but has no real endpoint.

package.json is a bloated corpse of unused deps and various unrelated tools that i cant find an active call for in the game files.

again, your tests folder is full of manual self-rolling tests for things like verifying DOM renders by checking for divs, but literally nothing to test for actual canvas rendering, hitboxes, camera placement, or anything else crucial to actual playability. this is mostly buld-ver boilerplate.

so much of the stuff you claimed to need custom backend for, or could've benfited from being wired in since you made one, isn't even passed through a server or any outside call logic. the economy stuff for insance is all computed/generated/displayed client-side in localStorage. this means that, as with many other things yo udon't want people getting their hands on, anyone can use browser devtools to modify in-game windows and bypass entire systems, rendering any sense of multiplayer unfair beyond a reasonable measure.

do not just willy nilly paste your API key into an LLM... speaking of which, ELEVENLABS\_API\_KEY and import.meta.env. are both hardcoded into multiple files. in fact, there are numerous places where you've hardcoded elements you shouldn't be passing client-side, which is what happens when you compile js/ts for webgl/3js builds like this. it would be very easy to pull a key or two. you "need" a backend, but your LLM didn't need to hard embed env client-side secrets.

and to speak again of bloat, there is SO much in your source code that doesn't need to be there, is effectively weighing down the entire system, badly wired, or routed to a very ineffective or potentially dangerous endpoint.

i think it's important to bring stuff like this to light because like with many other people posting barely covered ads for platforms/websites that want to drain user wallets, it's helpful to pinpoint exactly why this shit DOESN'T work the way people claim it does. again, you can work however you want to work on whatever you want to make, but if you don't understand the first thing about your codebase or how any of these systems talk to each other (or don't, in your case), then you are gonna have a 48 hour turnaround of a soupy mess of broken half-made games.

replies.author: anotherlebowski
replies.body:
So it sounds like what you're really arguing for is that AI is good at prototyping.  I honestly can't argue with that. It will get you something playable really fast.  Faster than I could code it, even with 15 years of experience.

The question is, once you decide "This loop is fun", how are you going to scale it?  More AI? Now you're taking this approach that you originally chose because it's fast and scaling it, which I worry is going to create a lot of hallucinations and sprawl that will feel soupy and wonky in a way that can be hard to articulate, but you know it right when you see it, much like an AI picture that looks a bit uncanny.  Except that's your game logic that's somewhat nonsensical.

You point out that the players don't care if the code is ugly.  You're right, but you should care because it makes your app hard to maintain. Anyone who has worked on a large codebase knows that once the game/app is big and messy it starts to get really hard to work with.  A bug pops up and you think "Jesus, I don't even know where to begin sleuthing around in this forest." So what's going to happen? Now you need to trust fall back into the AI's arms to solve the bug.  You've abstracted yourself out of the process.  You fundamentally don't know how the game works.  You know how you promoted it, and you know what's coming out the other side in playtests, but you don't know how the game actually works.  That's going to lead to so many bugs or unexpected mechanics that you don't even know exist.  

Look, maybe this is a new way to do it.  Maybe we want to abstract away how we interact with the computer, and maybe some day the tools will be good enough that we can. Maybe I'm a control freak because I want to know the actual logic of my "if...else" statements so I can confirm the game is doing what it's doing.  My gut feeling is just that the current tools build something vaguely similar to what was in my mind's eye, but they're not my actual vision.

replies.author: bingewavecinema

After you have decided the loop is fun, then and only then should you actually spend real resources and time on your game to make it really high quality. 

Think of games like Concord, $400 million spent over 8 years to fail in 11 days.

At this stage, the code base isn't that large, and if you've only spend 2-3 days or even a week or 2, you should no problem nor feelings scraping the entire thing, its not a huge loss.

replies.author: Houdinii1984
replies.body:
I mean, dev only = great games, AI only = some pretty good stuff, combine the two, and you're actually competitive. 

I don't see any malice in the post. It's a dev seeing the AI, and giving you exceptionally actionable information. Even if you're only in the AI realm, everything they said is stuff the AI should be handling or suggesting. If users can't run your game on their potato, they just won't.

If you're just mucking around, and such, it doesn't actually matter, but if you ever find something you want to continue, you'll sink faster than a mobster with concrete shoes because you only have experience iterating in a sandbox with artificial situations.

And if you're the type of person that learns on the fly and is fine with a slog, then that's once again a choice for you to make for yourself, which is great, but you'll verifiably have an easier time if you already know how it's supposed to go.

Like me? It's torture for me to undo work, so I go in with a specific way to do things to make the transition easier. I decided, and I execute. 

But you rage screaming 'WHO CARES' when your post makes it blatantly obvious that at least some people care because a metric fuck ton of people have been there before and already learned that lesson. You will at some point, too. When and how you do is your concern, but you treating people who offer you assistance or actionable information like they did something wrong is gonna make you look like the eternal beginner as everyone else learns the actual trade.

Its "WHO CARES" because if the goal is to validate how a core loops resonates, and its a person 2-3 days do it, they should have no qualms throwing the entire code base out, if it succeeds or fail. You're measuring the code at this stage, your measuring the ideas.

I'm been developing for 30 years since, since I was 12 and taught myself C++. Over my career, developers can focus on the wrong things, especially when they feel they are loosing control, so they hold on to what they have control over, the code.

This is the real content here!

AI tools are great for specific things, especially as an aid to people to learn a craft. Too many people see them instead as a shortcut. The things you note here are symptoms of someone who hasn't actually used AI to learn anything about what they are trying to create.

That being said, I can see part of OPs perspective. Despite the deficiencies in the game itself and the technical quality, they are describing an effort to tighten the loop between idea generation and validation, which does have merit. They produced a mock game to explore what a component of the game might feel like. That allows you to get closer to understanding the game itself, even if it's a technical mess under the hood. Looking at it in that light, it's not really transforming game development, but augmenting a subprocess of game development.

AI could be used to address all of the issues you bring up, but in the end I think the amount of time taken to address each of them with AI as a non-expert would be equivalent to, if not longer than, the time it would take to show this mockup to an actual developer and ask them to implement the game.

replies.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
replies.body:
> if you call yourself a multi decade pro in the field and then can’t even take the slightest bit of well intentioned criticism and just steamroll everyone who doesn’t fall in line with pure praise is just silly and doesn’t serve anyone.

I didn't really read much of what op wrote but if they're doing this, I don't believe they're in the industry. People who are in the industry long enough are usually confident but easily admit their limitations. This is usually the conditioning that come with being subject to code reviews.

You're absolutely correct. If you're getting feedback on exposed API key in your code... you're just bad, ignorant or indifferent.

You're spot on.

Just a side note. You probably don't need me to tell you this, but as team lead who is often responsible for hiring. Self taught developers are really fun to have. They're the "get it done" guys. If they're humble and open you can pair them with an architect or a someone with a senior with a lot of architectural knowledge... and you can go a LONG way.

This is because autodidact developers tend to learn by doing. So, they can learn a lot of bad habits BUT... they learned be finishing things or constructing thing. People with formal training, they tend very good with structure and the basics and theory. But they're not used to delivering full scope applications because they learn mostly by passing tests and assignments and those are fundamentally two different things.

So, kudos to you. It's not easy to learn something technical on your own.

replies.author: Puzzleheaded_Mix_811
replies.body:
Well I don't think you should bring up EA, they've been doing slop games without ai for at least 10 years. 

And the point is that RELEASING fast prototypes is the issue. Playing them by yourself, or showing them to your friends to get feedback sure.

But putting these on early access on steam or whatever platform, hoping that paying customers will play your 0.1, give you feedback, play your 0.2 that has been completely remade because you told prompt "here are the feedbacks, fix the game so it's better, make no mistake" and then keep iterating like that, this is just messed up on so many levels it's not even funny and the reason why I pointed OP at Soviet's essays, or any other essay that hammers the fact that you never get a second impression. 

This whole "here is my v0.01 which is barely more than an asset flip, please give feedback but don't be mean it's early access" trend was already bad enough  when the entry bar for such prototypes was high. Now that any random dude can do that kind of stuff with one hand in their pants in an afternoon after finding a few example prompts online and release this shit online, the market is going to be saturated with slop games and that will hurt the good indie games even more.
